cards.front: Bull vs. Bear
cards.back: Bull: investor who believes a market or security will rise in value (bullish). Bear: investor who believes a market or security will fall in value (bearish). A short seller is bearish.

cards.front: Bid price (in a quote)
cards.back: The highest price someone is currently willing to pay for a security. It is the price a seller receives. Size is expressed in round lots (100 shares).

cards.front: Ask (Offer) price
cards.back: The lowest price at which someone is currently willing to sell a security. It is the price a buyer pays. Size is expressed in round lots (100 shares).

cards.front: What is the 'inside quote' (inside market)?
cards.back: The highest available bid and the lowest available ask currently in the market for a security.

cards.front: BCO is quoted: bid 42 – ask 42.50, size 10 x 12. If a customer enters a market order to buy 500 shares, what price will the customer pay, and how many shares are available at that price?
cards.back: The customer buys at the ask = $42.50 per share. Up to 1,200 shares (12 round lots) are available at the ask. The 500-share order fills at $42.50.

cards.front: Three market makers quote MGS: GoldCoast 15.00–15.25 (15x20); Great Plains 15.20–15.27 (5x8); Seacoast 15.15–15.22 (10x12). What is the inside quote and size?
cards.back: Highest bid = 15.20 (Great Plains, size 5). Lowest ask = 15.22 (Seacoast, size 12). Inside quote: Bid 15.20 – Ask 15.22, size 5 x 12.

cards.front: What is the spread, and how does a market maker profit from it?
cards.back: The spread is the difference between the bid and ask prices. A market maker buys at the bid and sells at the ask, profiting from the spread (markup/markdown).

cards.front: How are bid and ask determined for exchange-listed stocks?
cards.back: The DMM maintains an order book of open limit orders. The highest buy limit sets the bid (and its size). The lowest sell limit sets the ask (and its size).

cards.front: Market order
cards.back: An order to buy or sell that is executed immediately at the best available market price. Market orders take precedence over limit orders and are filled first come, first served.

cards.front: Limit order
cards.back: An order with a specified maximum buy price or minimum sell price. Buy limit: execute at the limit or lower. Sell limit: execute at the limit or higher. Risk: the order may never be filled (missing the market).

cards.front: How does a stop order work?
cards.back: A stop order is not a live order — it is a trigger. When the stock trades at or through the stop price, the stop order becomes a market order and executes at the next available price. Stop orders have no time priority standing until triggered.

cards.front: How does a stop limit order differ from a stop order?
cards.back: Both are triggered when the stock trades at or through the stop price. A stop order then becomes a market order (guaranteed fill, not price). A stop limit order becomes a limit order (guaranteed price or better, not fill).

cards.front: BCO is trading at $12. A customer enters: Buy 2,000 BCO at 15 stop limit 16. Explain what happens.
cards.back: Once BCO trades at or through $15, the stop is triggered and the order becomes a buy limit order with a $16 limit. It will only execute at $16 or lower.

cards.front: ABC trades at $63. Julia wants to buy only if the price falls to $58 or lower. Which order type should she use?
cards.back: A buy limit order at $58. Buy limits execute at the limit price or lower, matching her requirement.

cards.front: Day order
cards.back: The default time restriction. Valid only until the close of trading on the day entered; any unexecuted portion is canceled at day's end.

cards.front: Good-til-canceled (GTC) order
cards.back: Valid until executed or canceled. All open GTC orders are automatically canceled on the last business day of April and the last business day of October unless renewed.

cards.front: Distinguish FOK, IOC, and AON orders.
cards.back: FOK (Fill-or-Kill): must be filled immediately and in full or canceled — no partials. IOC (Immediate-or-Cancel): fill immediately what you can; cancel the rest — partials allowed. AON (All-or-None): must be filled in full but not necessarily immediately; can be a day or GTC order. All three apply only to limit orders.

cards.front: Long position: buy/sell sequence, market view, and maximum loss?
cards.back: Buy to open, sell to close. Bullish (expects price to rise). Maximum loss = cost basis (if security becomes worthless).

cards.front: Short position: buy/sell sequence, market view, and maximum loss?
cards.back: Sell to open (borrowed shares), buy to close (cover). Bearish (expects price to fall). Maximum loss is unlimited because the stock price has no upside ceiling.

cards.front: Difference between a BD acting in agency vs. principal capacity?
cards.back: Agency (broker): trades on behalf of customers with another party; charges a commission. Principal (dealer/market maker): trades with the customer from its own inventory; profits on the spread (markup/markdown). A BD cannot act in both capacities on the same transaction.

cards.front: What is regular way settlement for Treasury securities vs. corporate, municipal, and agency securities?
cards.back: Treasury securities (T-bills, T-notes, T-bonds): T+1. Corporate stocks/bonds, municipal debt, agency (GNMA), and GSE (FNMA, FHLMC) securities: T+2.

cards.front: A customer buys 100 shares of ABC common stock on Thursday, June 30. July 4 is a holiday. When is settlement?
cards.back: Corporate stock settles T+2. Friday July 1 = T+1; Saturday/Sunday don't count; Monday July 4 is a holiday; Tuesday July 5 = T+2 (settlement date).

cards.front: What is cash (same-day) settlement?
cards.back: Settlement occurs on the trade date. Both buyer and seller must agree to cash settlement before the trade takes place. Not to be confused with a 'cash trade' (one without margin).

cards.front: Settlement for option trades vs. exercises?
cards.back: Option trade: T+1. Exercise of an equity option: T+2 (stock and cash delivered). Exercise of an index option: T+1 cash payment of intrinsic value (no underlying to deliver).

cards.front: What constitutes 'good delivery' of a physical stock certificate?
cards.back: The certificate must be endorsed (signed) by all owners listed on the face, with the signature matching the name exactly as it appears. A separate signed stock/bond power may be used instead and mailed separately for security.

cards.front: Street name
cards.back: Securities held electronically by a BD on behalf of a customer. No physical certificate exists and no physical signature is required for good delivery.
